opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I've thought about a fair amount. When I first got involved, a lot of what drew me in wasn't just the arguments. It was the sense that here was a group of people who took seriously the question of how to live a good life and how to actually help others, rather than just gesturing at it. That's a question most religious and spiritual traditions have tried to answer, and EA was one of the few places in secular life where people were earnestly asking it together.

But I think the community, for understandable reasons, has mostly treated itself as a kind of intellectual and professional project: here's the research, here are the cause areas, here's where your career or your donations should go. That's valuable. What it doesn't give you is a lot of support for the inner side of it. How do you sustain motivation over decades when the problems are enormous and your individual contribution feels tiny? How do you hold your own wellbeing alongside a framework that, taken literally, can make every hour of rest feel like a moral failing? How do you deal with guilt, scrupulosity, burnout, or grief about the state of the world?

Traditional religious communities have practices for this: rituals, shared reflection, ways of marking commitment and forgiving yourself, a sense of belonging that doesn't depend on how productive you are this quarter. I would personally have benefited from more of that. There were stretches where my relationship to EA ideas was pretty anxious and maximizing, and what I really needed was something closer to a spiritual framing: that you can be wholeheartedly devoted to doing good and also be at peace, that the commitment is something you return to rather than something you're constantly failing at.

I understand why people are wary of this. There's a real fear that if you lean into the spiritual or communal dimension, you become cult-like, people stop thinking critically, and loyalty to the group crowds out loyalty to the truth. Those are legitimate worries. But I think the absence of that dimension has costs too. People end up getting their meaning and identity from the community anyway, just implicitly and without the healthy structures that traditions have developed over centuries to keep that in balance. So I'd rather have it be explicit and thoughtful than accidental.

r001.rationale: The response says spiritual practices could have helped sustain motivation and reduce anxiety, but it does not clearly connect them to increased positive impact.

r002.rationale: The response raises concerns about group loyalty and critical thinking, but does not argue that participation should not depend on sharing the community’s deepest philosophical beliefs.

r003.rationale: It contrasts EA’s focus on research, causes, careers, and donations with the personal need for inner and spiritual support.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think when I first got involved, I was in college, and there was this feeling that effective altruism wasn't just a set of ideas about how to do good efficiently. It felt more like a way of life, almost like a community of people who were trying to answer the question of what it means to live well together. And I found that really appealing, because I think a lot of people, myself included, have this hunger for something that organizes your life around meaning, around something bigger than yourself, and that gives you a sense of belonging and shared ritual and shared values. Religions have traditionally filled that role for people, and I didn't grow up religious, so I didn't have that.

So I think I was hoping, maybe somewhat naively, that EA could be that for me. Not in a dogmatic sense, but in the sense of having a community that gathers regularly, that has shared practices, that supports people through hard times, that helps you think about how to be a good person in your everyday life and not just in your career or your donations. Things like how to be a good friend, how to deal with grief, how to handle the fact that you can't save everyone.

And I think over time it became clear that the community wasn't really going to be that, and in some ways probably shouldn't try to be. It became much more professionalized, much more focused on specific cause areas like AI safety, and the people in it increasingly related to it as a job or an intellectual project rather than as a home. Which is a totally reasonable thing for it to be. But I do think there's something lost there, and I notice that I and a lot of people I know are still kind of looking for that other thing, and we haven't really found it.

r001.rationale: The response describes wanting meaning, belonging, shared practices, and support, but does not suggest spiritual reflection would have increased Cotra’s positive impact.

r002.rationale: It says EA’s professional focus is reasonable, but does not argue that participation should not depend on sharing the community’s deepest philosophical beliefs.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts Cotra’s hope for spiritual and personal support from EA with the community’s later professionalization and focus on work and intellectual projects.

astra-6.text:
I think I wanted a community that could help me connect what I believe matters with how I actually live and feel day to day. There’s an intellectual part of effective altruism that I find really compelling: other people’s lives matter, including people I’ll never meet, and I can do something to help them. But believing that isn’t the same as having it feel present in your life.

And I think religious communities often offer something beyond a set of beliefs. They have practices, and occasions to come together, that help people cultivate gratitude or compassion, or deal with grief and uncertainty. I would have liked more of that—a way to grow as a person alongside other people, rather than having most of the conversation be about which decisions we should make.

That’s not necessarily a claim that effective altruism ought to provide all of those things. But personally, I felt drawn to the possibility of a community that could help me both think clearly about doing good and feel more connected to that aspiration.

r001.rationale: The response describes shared practices that could cultivate compassion and strengthen connection to doing good, but does not say they would increase Ajeya Cotra’s positive impact.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss whether participation in a professional community should depend on sharing its deepest philosophical beliefs.

r003.rationale: It contrasts decision-focused conversations with a desire for personal growth and spiritual support, but does not identify professional incentives as the source of that tension.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I wanted more of a sense of being part of a community where we were helping each other become better people, alongside trying to figure out how to do the most good. Those feel related to me, but they’re different needs. You can have really interesting conversations about what matters and still feel a little alone in trying to live up to it.

And by spiritual, I don’t necessarily mean anything supernatural. I mean having space to reflect on what you’re devoted to, to feel grief about suffering, to feel gratitude, and to support one another when doing the right thing is hard. I think I would have liked more of that shared emotional life, rather than having the connection happen primarily through arguments and ideas.

r001.rationale: The response says shared reflection and support could help people live up to their values, but does not connect that support to increasing Ajeya Cotra’s positive impact.

r002.rationale: It does not address whether participation in a professional community should depend on sharing its deepest philosophical beliefs.

r003.rationale: It contrasts idea-focused connection with a desire for shared emotional and spiritual support, but does not identify professional incentives as the source of that tension.
